title: Reflection
text:
This portfolio reflects my transition from a consulting and project management background into a more analytics-focused role.
It demonstrates not only the development of technical skills, but also my ability to apply data-driven thinking to real business problems.



Throughout this module, I developed practical skills in:

Python for data analysis

exploratory data analysis and statistical thinking

machine learning fundamentals

More importantly, I learned how to connect technical analysis with business context

In the fraud detection project, I explored how data can support risk identification and decision-making

In the NLP project, I worked with unstructured text data and compared AI approaches, gaining insight into model strengths and limitations

This shift from technical execution to business-oriented analysis was a key part of my development.
This transition required a shift in mindset, from focusing on delivery and execution to thinking critically about data, interpretation, and decision-making.



One of the main challenges was working with machine learning models such as BERT.

Initially, I found it difficult to understand how text is processed and how models can be applied in practice

I addressed this by breaking down the workflow step-by-step and focusing on core concepts rather than complexity

Another challenge was handling performance and technical constraints when working with large models.

I simplified the implementation

Reduced dataset size where necessary

Focused on meaningful outputs rather than computational complexity

I also faced challenges in building the portfolio using Quarto.

Learning how to structure files, manage YAML configuration, and debug rendering issues was an important part of the process

These challenges helped me become more confident in both technical implementation and problem-solving.
Before this module, I viewed analytics mainly as reporting and data processing. This experience changed my perspective, showing that analytics is fundamentally about interpreting data to support decisions.



This experience highlighted several important lessons:

Technical accuracy alone is not enough — clear communication of results is equally important

Simpler, well-structured models can often be more effective than complex approaches

Understanding the business problem is critical when selecting analytical methods

Model performance must always be interpreted in context, not just reported

My consulting background helped me approach analytics problems in a structured and business-oriented way




Going forward, I plan to strengthen my skills in:

advanced machine learning techniques

feature engineering and model evaluation

data visualisation and dashboard development

applying analytics to real-world business problems

While I have built a strong foundation, I recognise that further experience is needed to apply advanced models at scale and in real-world production environments.
This portfolio represents an important step in developing a strong foundation for a career in data analytics.

title: Clinic Appointment No-Show Analysis
text:
This project examines patient appointment data to understand patterns behind missed clinic appointments.
The analysis combines SQL-based data cleaning, KPI calculation, segmentation, and business interpretation to identify which factors are most strongly associated with no-shows.

title: Clinic Appointment No-Show Analysis
text:
This project examines patient appointment data to understand patterns behind missed clinic appointments.
The analysis combines SQL-based data cleaning, KPI calculation, segmentation, and business interpretation to identify which factors are most strongly associated with no-shows.

title: Clinic Appointment No-Show Analysis
text:
Business Problem
Missed appointments create operational inefficiency in healthcare settings. They waste clinical capacity, increase waiting times, and reduce service effectiveness.
The goal of this project was to identify key factors linked to appointment no-shows and generate practical recommendations that could help clinics improve attendance.

title: Clinic Appointment No-Show Analysis
text:
Dataset
The dataset contains over 110,000 medical appointments. The target variable is no_show:

1 = missed appointment
0 = attended appointment

The dataset includes appointment timing, patient demographics, neighbourhood, chronic condition indicators, SMS reminder status, and attendance outcome.
Initial data checks showed that the dataset required cleaning before analysis, including removal of one invalid age value and records with impossible waiting times.

title: Clinic Appointment No-Show Analysis
text:
Key Findings
The overall no-show rate was approximately 20%, meaning around 1 in 5 appointments were missed.
Waiting time showed a strong relationship with attendance. Patients with short waiting times had much lower no-show rates than those waiting longer.
Age was also important. Patients aged 18–30 showed the highest no-show rates, while patients over 50 had lower rates.
Gender did not show a meaningful difference in no-show behaviour.






NoteKey Insight



The highest-risk group was younger patients with longer waiting times and no SMS reminder.
This suggests that clinics should focus on targeted intervention rather than applying the same reminder strategy to all patients.

title: Clinic Appointment No-Show Analysis
text:
Business Interpretation
The findings suggest that no-shows are influenced more by operational and behavioural factors than by simple demographic characteristics such as gender.
The strongest opportunities for improvement are reducing waiting time and focusing reminder efforts on higher-risk patient groups.

title: Clinic Appointment No-Show Analysis
text:
Recommendations

Reduce waiting time where possible
Prioritise reminder strategies for younger patients
Target high-risk segments rather than treating all patients the same
Monitor waiting-time driven attendance risk as a core KPI

text:
This project examines fraud patterns in customer transaction data and evaluates whether fraud can be predicted using customer and transaction-related variables.
The analysis combines exploratory data analysis, statistical testing, outlier detection, and predictive modeling to understand which factors are associated with fraud and whether they can support fraud detection.

title: Fraud Pattern Analysis and Predictive Modeling
text:
This project examines fraud patterns in customer transaction data and evaluates whether fraud can be predicted using customer and transaction-related variables.
The analysis combines exploratory data analysis, statistical testing, outlier detection, and predictive modeling to understand which factors are associated with fraud and whether they can support fraud detection.

title: Fraud Pattern Analysis and Predictive Modeling
text:
Business Problem
Fraud detection is an important part of financial risk management. Organizations need to identify suspicious activity as early as possible to reduce losses and improve prevention strategies.
The goal of this project was to determine whether customer characteristics and transaction-related variables could reliably distinguish fraudulent from non-fraudulent activity.

title: Fraud Pattern Analysis and Predictive Modeling
text:
Dataset
The dataset contains 500 rows and 23 columns. The target variable is is_fraud:

1 = fraud
0 = non-fraud

The dataset includes customer, financial, and transaction-related variables such as age, income, credit score, loan amount, transaction amount, device type, and transaction type.
Initial data checks showed no missing values, no duplicates, and a balanced fraud distribution.

title: Fraud Pattern Analysis and Predictive Modeling
text:
Analytical Approach
The project followed a structured workflow:

Data understanding
Data cleaning and preparation
Exploratory data analysis
Outlier detection
Confidence interval analysis
Hypothesis testing
Predictive modeling (Logistic Regression)

title: Fraud Pattern Analysis and Predictive Modeling
text:
Model Selection Rationale
Logistic Regression was selected as a baseline model due to its interpretability and suitability for binary classification problems. It allows for clear understanding of how input variables influence fraud prediction, which is important in risk-sensitive business contexts.

title: Fraud Pattern Analysis and Predictive Modeling
text:
Key Findings
Most variables did not strongly differentiate fraud from non-fraud cases.
Variables such as transaction amount, loan amount, credit score, region, and device type showed weak or no clear relationship with fraud.
The only variable showing a statistically significant difference was personal income, with fraud cases associated with lower income levels.






NoteKey Insight



The analysis showed that traditional demographic and financial variables were not strong predictors of fraud.
This highlights the importance of behavioural patterns and transaction-level data in building effective fraud detection systems.

title: Fraud Pattern Analysis and Predictive Modeling
text:
Model Performance
Logistic Regression results:

Accuracy: 0.61
Precision: 0.58
Recall: 0.69
ROC-AUC: 0.61

These results suggest limited predictive power using the available features.

title: Fraud Pattern Analysis and Predictive Modeling
text:
Limitations
The model performance is constrained by the dataset size and the type of features available. The dataset primarily includes static attributes, which limits the ability to capture behavioural fraud patterns.

title: Fraud Pattern Analysis and Predictive Modeling
text:
Business Interpretation
Fraud detection cannot rely only on demographic or financial variables.
More effective approaches should focus on:

behavioral indicators
unusual transaction patterns
device and login activity

title: Fraud Pattern Analysis and Predictive Modeling
text:
Recommendations

Focus on behavioral fraud signals
Improve data collection with richer features
Monitor large financial outliers
Retrain models regularly

The model achieved moderate performance, with stronger recall than precision. This indicates that the model was more effective at identifying fraud cases than avoiding false positives.
In a fraud detection context, higher recall is often preferred, as missing fraudulent transactions can lead to significant financial loss. However, the relatively low precision suggests that many flagged transactions may not actually be fraudulent, which could increase operational costs.

title: Fraud Pattern Analysis and Predictive Modeling
text:
Business Impact
These findings suggest that organizations should:

shift from static rule-based systems to behavior-based detection
invest in richer transaction-level data
continuously retrain models with updated patterns

For organizations, this means that investment in richer behavioural and transaction-level data is likely to deliver more value than relying only on static customer attributes.

Model Selection Rationale

Limitations
The performance of both models is influenced by the quality and structure of the dataset. Neutral sentiment was particularly difficult to classify, likely due to ambiguity in labeling.
Additionally, GPT performance depends heavily on prompt design, which introduces variability and reduces consistency compared to supervised approaches.
